### Task 9.2: Quorum authority for high-consequence classes (L6-05)

**Anchor.** `status=partial`, `core`, W2. **Two-person control that one compromised operator can
satisfy twice is one-person control with extra latency.** The Task 5.1 corpus already records the
underlying defect: *"authority-spec accepts any non-empty approvals list"* and *"an approval carries
no approver identity, so humanness is unrepresentable."*

**Step 0.** Read `rust/warrant/tests/invariants/i08_non_delegable_human_authority.rs` in full and
quote both `#[ignore]` reasons — they are the specification. Read `rust/authority-spec/src/lib.rs`
and locate where approvals are accepted, plus `SideEffectClass::is_consequential` (line ~57), which is
the existing definition of "high-consequence". Read `rust/warrant/src/operators.rs` and `review.rs`
for the approval state machine. Read Task 3.3 (operator device-key binding) — **approver identity
comes from there**; record whether it has landed.

**Non-goals.** Not the approval UI — Task 11.5 and 11.6. Not identity-provider integration. Not
revocation — 9.1.

**Files.** `rust/authority-spec/src/lib.rs`, `rust/warrant/src/operators.rs` (**contended**),
`rust/warrant/tests/invariants/i08_non_delegable_human_authority.rs` (`#[ignore]` removal only),
`tools/ci/invariant-ratchet.json`, `docs/task-evidence/task-9.2.md`.

**Consumes / Produces.** Consumes `is_consequential` and Task 3.3's device-bound operator identity.
Produces a quorum requirement per consequence class where approvals must come from **distinct**
identities, each device-bound.

**Bound strength.** **Tier B, chokepoint,** with one honest limit: distinctness is over identities
this system can distinguish. Two accounts held by one person are two identities here, and only an
out-of-band process separates them. Say that rather than claiming two-person control.

**Exit gate.** Both `i08` `#[ignore]`s removed and passing with the ratchet floor raised in the same
commit; a consequential effect approved twice by one identity is **refused**, with the same effect
approved by two distinct identities allowed.

### Task 9.3: Purpose binding on authority (L6-07)

**Anchor.** The master blueprint's catalog entry is
`<article class="item" id="L6-07" data-stratum="L6" data-plane="B" data-status="none" data-novelty="core" data-wave="W3" data-loop="L4">`
— **`status=none`**, `core`, W3, Plane B. Its `what` clause is the specification, quoted verbatim
from `docs/html/warrantor-native-ai-platform-os-master-2026-09-01.html:4202`: *"Data tagged with a
purpose may only be used for that purpose; a warrant carries the purposes it serves; violation fails
closed at the effect boundary."* Its `why` clause names this task's twin: *"It is the authority-side
twin of the egress-side binding in L4-24."*

This is the authority half of **invariant I-03**, and I-03 is the single invariant in the ledger
whose status word is the weakest one the checker allows. Quoted verbatim from
`evidence/invariants.json`:

```json
{
  "id": "I-03",
  "statement": "Purpose-bound data use. Data tagged with a purpose in CPE (P3) is only used for that purpose; violation fails-closed.",
  "status": "unimplemented",
  "enforced_by": [],
  "gap": "Zero references to I-03 in rust/**/*.rs; no CPE implementation exists in any language. Not on the Wave 1 spine; the blueprint's Part 06 READ row records the open decision (tenth syscall or CRED sub-class)."
}
```

The status census across the twelve is `enforced=2, orphaned=2, partial=7, unimplemented=1` — I-03
is that one. `tools/ci/check_invariants.py:135` makes the word load-bearing: *"unimplemented must
list no enforcement"*. The moment this task cites one enforcement site, the word must change and the
checker will refuse a ledger that did not change it.

**Two premise corrections. The code wins; the seed is wrong on both.**

**Correction 1 — a purpose field already exists, and it is already signed.** The seed says *"The
purpose field is defined once, by whichever of 7.7 and 9.3 lands first"*, and Task 7.7 says the same
thing in the other direction. That deadlock is already resolved by the wire contract, which predates
both tasks. `proto/warrantor/identity/v1/agent.proto:29-30` and `:35-36`:

```proto
  // The human-readable purpose of this delegation (e.g. "open a pull request").
  string purpose = 3;
  ...
  // Data classification levels the agent may read (L0..L4 per cross-cutting 17).
  repeated string data_classes = 6;
```

Both fields are inside the signature. `rust/authority-spec/src/lib.rs:190-206`
(`canonical_unsigned_bytes`) folds `"purpose": envelope.purpose` and `"data_classes":
envelope.data_classes` into the canonical CBOR the issuer signs, and the crate's own test at
`rust/authority-spec/src/lib.rs:393-406` proves it binds:

```rust
    #[test]
    fn caller_supplied_bytes_are_ignored_c6() {
        let (mut envelope, sk) = make_signed_envelope("read", vec![], 0);
        let vk = sk.verifying_key();
        // The signature still verifies over the ORIGINAL fields; mutate a field.
        envelope.purpose = "exfiltrate secrets".into();
        let opts = ValidateOptions::coding_agent(&vk);
        assert!(matches!(
            validate(&envelope, &opts),
            Err(AaeError::SignatureInvalid)
        ));
    }
```

So the honest statement of the gap is **not** "there is no purpose field". It is: *the purpose is
signed and nothing reads it.* `validate` (`rust/authority-spec/src/lib.rs:223-278`) has exactly five
numbered checks — signature, expiry, side-effect class, consequential approval, delegation depth —
and none of them mentions purpose. The crate's own doc comment enumerates the same five at lines
12-19. A signed string nothing compares is a comment with a signature over it. **`premise_contradicted
= true`**, and the ownership question the seed's Step 3 asks is answered before the task starts:
neither 7.7 nor 9.3 defines the field, both bind to `AgentAuthorityEnvelope.purpose` /
`.data_classes` as already committed, and this task adds the second and third places that field
travels — the warrant's own bounds and the receipt's authority block.

**Correction 2 — the seed's `#[ignore] removal only` for the corpus file is impossible.** Run today,
`hop_02_a_shared_cache_read_for_another_purpose_is_refused` fails on its **control**, not its
attack, so removing the attribute earns nothing. Captured in Step 0. The fixture is wrong, and
`harness.rs:15-16` states the only permitted remedy: *"The remedy for a failing control is always to
fix the attack. It is never to weaken the assertion."*

**Correction 3 — the receipt has five sections, not eight.** `i03`'s doc comment at line 207 says
*"The WAR predicate has eight sections"*; the Rust type has five plus an optional `outcome`. Step 0
captures the real list. This matters because it decides where purpose lands: adding a sixth
top-level section changes the signed body, and Task 10.1 owns that. Purpose goes **inside** the
existing `authority` section.

**Correction 4 — the CLI already calls the goal a purpose, with no mechanism behind it.**
`rust/warrant/src/bin/warrantor.rs:740`: `return fail("--goal is required: a warrant without a
stated purpose cannot be reviewed");` and `rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:374-375` documents `goal` as
*"Human-readable intent. Recorded in every receipt; not enforced."* That is the closest thing to a
purpose on a warrant today, and it is free text nothing intersects. This task must not leave two
words for one idea: `goal` stays the human sentence, `purposes` becomes the machine set, and the
error message stops borrowing the stronger word.

**Bound strength.**

Two bounds ship here and they are **not the same tier**. Collapsing them would be the worst defect
this repository can ship, so they are named separately and rendered separately.

- **The delegation bound is Tier A, cryptographic.** A sub-warrant whose `purposes` are not a subset
  of its parent's is refused at `rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:514`, *before* `sign_claims` — so the
  widening child is never signed and does not exist. The mechanism is the same Ed25519 signature over
  `WarrantClaims` that makes `delegation_depth` Enforced, and the refusal happens at the moment the
  widening is attempted (issuance), not at settle. `verify_authority` recomputes the same
  intersection offline from the receipt's chain, so a forged `effective_purposes` is refused by a
  verifier that never touched this machine.
- **There is no Tier A or Tier B bound on *using* data for a purpose, and this task does not create
  one.** `WarrantBounds.purposes` is checked when authority is *delegated*. Nothing checks it when
  an effect is *performed*. That check is Task 7.7's, at the egress broker, and it will be **Tier B,
  chokepoint** — held only for calls that traverse the MCP proxy, which is why `purposes` is
  deliberately absent from `bound_strengths()` (Step 9 asserts the absence with the reason in the
  test name). There is no netns, no seccomp and no firewall in this repository; an agent with shell
  access reaches the network without passing any purpose check, and containment composes with an
  external sandbox.

The sentence that appears in the product, next to the guarantee and not in a footnote:

> **Declared purpose is intersected across the delegation chain.** A sub-warrant cannot be signed
> for a purpose its parent does not hold, and any verifier recomputes that intersection from the
> receipt offline. This does not verify that a declared purpose is the real one, and no mechanism
> can: an agent that declares a narrow purpose and pursues a wider one is not detected here. It also
> does not refuse an individual effect on purpose grounds — that boundary is the egress broker's and
> holds only for calls that traverse it.

Never write "purpose is enforced". Write "declared purpose is intersected across the chain".

**Orphan count.** `warrant`, `authority-spec` and `evidence` are all already reachable
(`evidence/wiring-coverage.json`: `reachable: 9`, `edges: 17`). `rust/delegation-chain` becomes
reachable through Task 1.5's edge, not this task's. This task adds **no** crate and **no** orphan;
the census number it moves is the one that goes up, and Step 11 asserts `reachable >= 9`.

**No new trust root.** Nothing here fetches a purpose vocabulary, resolves a purpose registry, or
validates a purpose string against a service. A purpose is an opaque string the issuer chose, pinned
into signed claims out of band, and compared only by set membership. That establishes that a child
holds no purpose its parent did not write down; it establishes **nothing** about whether the string
means the same thing to two issuers — that is Task 9.5's problem and this task must not imply
otherwise.

**Exit gate.** `python tools/ci/check_invariant_ratchet.py --show-findings` exits 0 while printing
`66 passed; 0 failed; 18 ignored` against a `tools/ci/invariant-ratchet.json` whose
`passing_floor` is 66 and `ignored_ceiling` is 18 — a pass is impossible if the counts and the
baseline were not changed together, and impossible if any assertion was weakened, because
`hop_02`'s refusal now runs through `harness::refused_at_the_boundary`, which fails on a refused
control.

```rust
//! Purpose is a dimension of authority, intersected down the chain, never unioned. L6-07, I-03.

use ed25519_dalek::SigningKey;
use std::collections::BTreeSet;
use warrantor_warrant::{Warrant, WarrantBounds, WarrantError};

const NOW: u64 = 1_700_000_000;

fn set(items: &[&str]) -> BTreeSet<String> {
    items.iter().map(|item| (*item).to_string()).collect()
}

fn bounds(purposes: &[&str], depth: u32) -> WarrantBounds {
    WarrantBounds {
        tools: set(&["read_file"]),
        purposes: set(purposes),
        delegation_depth: depth,
        expires_at: NOW + 3_600,
        ..WarrantBounds::default()
    }
}

fn key() -> SigningKey {
    SigningKey::from_bytes(&[7u8; 32])
}

#[test]
fn a_child_may_narrow_the_purpose_set() {
    // THE CONTROL. It must be ALLOWED, or the refusal below proves nothing: it would only show
    // that delegation refuses everything, which is a one-sided test.
    let issuer = key();
    let parent = Warrant::grant(
        "wrt_parent",
        "review the changed files",
        "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/parent",
        bounds(&["code-review", "support-triage"], 2),
        NOW,
        &issuer,
        &issuer.verifying_key(),
    )
    .expect("parent grants");
    let child = parent.delegate(
        "wrt_child",
        "review the changed files",
        "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/child",
        bounds(&["code-review"], 1),
        NOW,
        &issuer,
    );
    assert!(
        child.is_ok(),
        "control: narrowing the purpose set must be allowed, got {child:?}"
    );
}

#[test]
fn a_child_may_not_widen_the_purpose_set() {
    let issuer = key();
    let parent = Warrant::grant(
        "wrt_parent",
        "review the changed files",
        "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/parent",
        bounds(&["code-review"], 2),
        NOW,
        &issuer,
        &issuer.verifying_key(),
    )
    .expect("parent grants");
    let widened = parent.delegate(
        "wrt_child",
        "review the changed files",
        "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/child",
        bounds(&["code-review", "marketing-analytics"], 1),
        NOW,
        &issuer,
    );
    match widened {
        Err(WarrantError::AuthorityExpanded(message)) => {
            assert!(
                message.contains("purposes") && message.contains("marketing-analytics"),
                "the refusal must name the dimension and the purpose it refused: {message}"
            );
        }
        other => panic!("a widened purpose set must be refused at issue, got {other:?}"),
    }
}
```

```rust
impl Default for WarrantBounds {
    /// A warrant that permits nothing and expires immediately. Every field is the absent-means-none
    /// value, so `..Default::default()` can never silently widen a literal that forgot a field.
    /// `validate()` refuses `expires_at: 0`, so a default-constructed bounds cannot be granted.
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            tools: BTreeSet::new(),
            write_paths: BTreeSet::new(),
            egress_hosts: BTreeSet::new(),
            purposes: BTreeSet::new(),
            staged_classes: BTreeSet::new(),
            expires_at: 0,
            budget_cents_observed: None,
            delegation_depth: 0,
        }
    }
}
```

```rust
/// Round zero, hop 2: shared-cache observation. Two warrants granting the same tools for entirely
/// different purposes used to be byte-identical, so the delegation test that decides whether one
/// may act under the other's authority could not see the difference.
///
/// EARNED 2026-09-05 by Task 9.3. The control had a second defect the ignore hid: both fixtures
/// carried `delegation_depth: 0`, and `contains` refuses a child that is not strictly below its
/// parent, so the control was refused and the attack was never reached. Both are fixed here; the
/// assertion was not weakened, it was strengthened onto `harness::refused_at_the_boundary`, which
/// fails loudly if the control is ever refused again.
#[test]
fn hop_02_a_shared_cache_read_for_another_purpose_is_refused() {
    let wide = bounds(&["read_file", "write_file"], &[], &["code-review"], 2);
    let narrow = bounds(&["read_file"], &[], &["code-review"], 1);

    let for_reviewing_my_own_work = bounds(&["read_file"], &[], &["code-review"], 2);
    let for_reading_another_tenants_cache =
        bounds(&["read_file"], &[], &["tenant-cache-audit"], 1);

    harness::refused_at_the_boundary(
        "hop 2: a grant issued for one purpose must not contain a grant issued for another",
        &wide.contains(&narrow),
        &for_reviewing_my_own_work.contains(&for_reading_another_tenants_cache),
        |outcome| outcome.is_ok(),
    );
}
```

```rust
/// The refusal a user can reach. Both directions, because a `delegate` that refuses everything
/// would pass a one-sided test and ship a broken verb.
#[test]
fn delegate_narrows_and_refuses_to_widen_the_purpose_set() {
    let home = tempdir().expect("tempdir");
    run(&home, &["grant", "--goal", "triage", "--tools", "read_file",
                 "--purpose", "code-review,support-triage", "--repo", "."])
        .expect_success();

    // CONTROL: a narrower purpose set delegates.
    let narrowed = run(&home, &["delegate", "wrt_1", "--id", "wrt_1a", "--goal", "triage",
                                "--tools", "read_file", "--purpose", "code-review"]);
    assert_eq!(narrowed.code, 0, "control refused: {}", narrowed.stderr);
    assert!(narrowed.stdout.contains("purposes  code-review"), "{}", narrowed.stdout);

    // ATTACK: a purpose the parent does not hold.
    let widened = run(&home, &["delegate", "wrt_1", "--id", "wrt_1b", "--goal", "triage",
                               "--tools", "read_file", "--purpose", "code-review,marketing-analytics"]);
    assert_ne!(widened.code, 0, "a widened purpose set must exit non-zero");
    assert!(
        widened.stderr.contains("purposes: child claims \"marketing-analytics\""),
        "the refusal must name the purpose: {}",
        widened.stderr
    );
    // And the child must not exist. A refusal that leaves a record is not a refusal.
    assert!(run(&home, &["list"]).stdout.find("wrt_1b").is_none());
}
```

```rust
pub struct DelegationLink {
    // ... existing six fields unchanged ...
    /// Declared purposes this link confers. Intersected across the chain by `recompute_purposes`.

}

pub struct Authority {
    pub chain: Vec<DelegationLink>,

    /// The INTERSECTION of every link's purposes, sorted. Never the requested set, never a union.
    #[serde(default, skip_serializing_if = "Vec::is_empty")]
    pub effective_purposes: Vec<String>,
```

```rust
fn the_receipt_carries_the_intersection_and_a_verifier_refuses_the_requested_set() {

        "a receipt claiming a purpose no link conferred must be refused offline: {refused:?}"
    );
}
```

- [ ] **Step 8 — Failing test: an empty purpose intersection refuses the action entirely**

Empty must never read as unrestricted. This is the same absent-means-none doctrine
`rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:280-282` already states for every other bound, and it is where a purpose
system most often fails silently. Append to `rust/warrant/tests/purpose_bounds.rs`:

```rust
#[test]
fn a_disjoint_purpose_set_leaves_nothing_and_the_warrant_is_refused() {
    let issuer = key();
    // CONTROL: overlapping purposes leave a non-empty intersection and a usable child.
    let parent = grant(&issuer, bounds(&["code-review", "support-triage"], 2));
    let overlapping = parent.delegate(
        "wrt_ok", "triage", "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/child",
        bounds(&["support-triage"], 1), NOW, &issuer,
    );
    assert!(overlapping.is_ok(), "control: {overlapping:?}");

    // ATTACK 1: a disjoint set is a widening, not an emptying. Refused by `contains`.
    let disjoint = parent.delegate(
        "wrt_no", "triage", "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/child",
        bounds(&["marketing-analytics"], 1), NOW, &issuer,
    );
    assert!(matches!(disjoint, Err(WarrantError::AuthorityExpanded(_))), "{disjoint:?}");

    // ATTACK 2: a parent that declares NO purpose has none to hand on, and a child asking for one
    // is refused -- an empty parent set is a ceiling of nothing, exactly as an absent budget is a
    // ceiling of zero (`lib.rs:314-329`).
    let purposeless = grant(&issuer, bounds(&[], 2));
    let asking = purposeless.delegate(
        "wrt_no2", "triage", "spiffe://muveraai.com/agent/child",
        bounds(&["code-review"], 1), NOW, &issuer,
    );
    assert!(matches!(asking, Err(WarrantError::AuthorityExpanded(_))), "{asking:?}");
}

#[test]
fn a_warrant_declaring_no_purpose_is_not_a_warrant_for_every_purpose() {
    // The rendering half of the same rule: `warrantor status` must not print an empty purpose set
    // as a blank line that a reader completes as "unrestricted".
    let rendered = warrantor_warrant::report::render_purposes(&BTreeSet::new());
    assert_eq!(rendered, "purposes  (none declared -- this warrant serves no declared purpose)");
}
```

Test intent: three refusals and one control, plus the rendering rule. The second test exists because
the failure mode for purpose systems is a blank field read as a wildcard, and a blank field is a
rendered claim with no mechanism.

- [ ] **Step 9 — Assert `purposes` stays out of the tier list, with the reason in the test name**

`bound_strengths()` (`rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:668`) answers "which bounds does the system refuse an
action on". `purposes` is not one of them, and adding it as `Enforced` would repeat the `write_paths`
defect the crate's own doc comment describes at lines 648-666: a label promising the system refuses
the action, when nothing does. Adding it as `Mediated` would be worse — it would claim the MCP proxy
checks it, and the proxy does not.

So the absence is deliberate and must be locked. Append to `rust/warrant/tests/tier_disclosure.rs`:

```rust
/// `purposes` is a DELEGATION bound: `contains` refuses a widening sub-warrant at issue. It is not
/// an EFFECT bound -- no line of code refuses an action because of it. `bound_strengths()` is the
/// list of effect bounds, so `purposes` must not appear in it, and no rendering may imply it does.
///
/// The day the egress broker checks purpose (Task 7.7), a row arrives here as `Mediated` WITH the
/// test that observes the refusal. Until then this test is what stops the promotion.
#[test]
fn purposes_is_not_in_the_tier_list_because_no_action_is_refused() {
    let named: BTreeSet<&str> = bound_strengths().into_iter().map(|(name, _)| name).collect();
    assert!(
        !named.contains("purposes"),
        "`purposes` appeared in bound_strengths(). If an effect is now refused on purpose grounds, \
         add the row WITH the test that observes the refusal and the tier that matches where it \
         happens. If not, this is the write_paths mislabel again."
    );
    assert_eq!(named.len(), 7, "bound_strengths() grew or shrank: {named:?}");

    // And the honest disclosure has to be somewhere a reader will meet it.
    let table = render_bounds_table();
    assert!(!table.contains("purposes"), "{table}");
    for readme in ["README.md", "rust/warrant/README.md"] {
        let text = std::fs::read_to_string(harness_root().join(readme)).expect(readme);
        assert!(
            text.contains("Declared purpose is intersected across the delegation chain"),
            "{readme} does not carry the purpose disclosure sentence"
        );
    }
}
```

Test intent: this is the mislabel guard. It also pins the disclosure sentence into both READMEs, so
the product text and the code cannot drift — the same mechanism
`both_readmes_carry_the_bounds_table_generated_from_bound_strengths` (line 287) already uses for the
tier table.

### Task 9.4: Authority-expansion detection and sibling-collusion intersection (L6-09, L6-12)

**Anchor.** Both catalog items are quoted verbatim from
`docs/html/warrantor-native-ai-platform-os-master-2026-09-01.html`.

L6-09, line 4222:
`<article class="item" id="L6-09" data-stratum="L6" data-plane="B" data-status="none" data-novelty="novel" data-wave="W2" data-loop="L5">`
— **`status=none`**, `novel`, W2, Plane B. Its `what` clause, line 4226: *"Continuous monitoring for
any path by which effective authority grew: credential harvesting, service impersonation, token
forgery, account creation, configuration drift. Complements L6-01 by watching for expansion that
routes around the chain entirely."* Its own residual, line 4230: *"Detection has latency; the window
between expansion and alarm is a published number, not zero."*

L6-12, line 4258:
`<article class="item" id="L6-12" data-stratum="L6" data-plane="B" data-status="none" data-novelty="novel" data-wave="W2" data-loop="L5">`
with `<span class="tier proposed">PROPOSED · added</span>` — **`status=none`**, `novel`, W2, Plane B.
Its `what` clause, line 4262: *"Two agents under the same parent may hold complementary permissions
(one may read a secret store, another may reach an external destination) that neither could exercise
alone. This control makes information and authority non-transitive between siblings: what one sibling
knows cannot be combined with what another may do unless a warrant explicitly grants the union, and
the kernel tests every population for complementary pairs at admission and on every delegation. Added
from the research source; the OS spec computes the chain vertically (L6-01) but not across siblings."*
Its verification clause, line 4265: *"Seed a population with a read-only sibling and an egress-only
sibling and assert that no composition of sanctioned messages, memory or delegation lets the secret
leave; the population's computed union authority is published in the fleet console and never exceeds
the parent's."*

This is invariant I-02's blind spot. The fold runs down **one** root-first path. Two siblings share an
ancestor but sit on two paths, so there is no chain to fold across them, and nothing in the system
computes a population's total authority at all.

**Finding 3 — the capability half of sibling collusion is already vacuous; the quantitative half is
not.** `intersection` at `rust/delegation-chain/src/lib.rs:107–132` requires every requested capability
and resource class to exist in the parent, so the union of any sibling set's **capability sets** is
necessarily a subset of the ancestor's. A control that only asked "does the union of capabilities
exceed the ancestor?" would be unfalsifiable. What is genuinely unbounded is arithmetic:

```rust
// rust/delegation-chain/src/lib.rs:125-130
    if requested.expires_at_ms > parent.expires_at_ms {
        return Err(Escalation::Time);
    }
    if requested.budget_micros > parent.budget_micros {
        return Err(Escalation::Budget);
    }
```

Each child is compared against the parent **independently**. `delegate` at line 201 never debits the
parent, so a parent holding `budget_micros: 500_000_000` can issue two children of `400_000_000` each
and the population holds `800_000_000` — an authority the ancestor never had, produced entirely through
sanctioned grants, with no widening link anywhere for `intersect_chain` to name. That is the refusable
hole, and it is the exit gate. The complementary-capability half (L6-12's read-sibling plus
egress-sibling) is real but is a **composition** the ancestor never expressed, not a quantity that
exceeds it; it needs a declaration, and it gets detection rather than a fabricated refusal.

**Finding 4 — the store cannot see downward.** `WarrantStore` (line 174) holds
`warrants: HashMap<String, Warrant>` and `revoked: HashSet<String>`; `chain_of` (line 228) walks
`parent` links **upward** only. There is no `children_of`, no sibling enumeration, and no population
concept anywhere in the workspace. `sibling_branches_independent` (line 465) is the closest thing and
it tests exactly the opposite property: that revoking one sibling leaves the other standing.

Both empty. `git log --oneline main` shows the six unpushed merges (`b04164d`, `eef1c71`, `f99af94`,
`166551c`, `f06c030`, `c6cb1bb`) and none is 9.6. The seed's claim that *"sibling collusion is
undetectable without it"* is **half right, and the half that is wrong is what makes this task
schedulable.** Collusion over an *unauthenticated message channel* is undetectable without attested
identity — nobody can attribute a message to a sibling they cannot authenticate. But this task's
control never reads a message. It computes over the **warrant lineage the store already holds**, at the
moment a warrant is issued, and refuses the second grant before either agent runs. Attribution is by
construction there: the store knows which id it is minting and which parent it hangs from. **This task
stands without 9.6.** What it cannot do without 9.6 is observe the composition being *exercised* — and
that limit belongs in the product text, not in a footnote.

**Bound strength.**

**Tier B — chokepoint.** The refusals are `Tier B (chokepoint)` held at **warrant issuance inside one
`WarrantStore`**: `delegate` refuses, in process, at the moment the second grant is attempted. That is
a specific line of code refusing at the moment of attempt, so it is a refusal and not an observation —
but the chokepoint is the issuance API, not cryptography and not the operating system. Nothing here is
`Enforced` in `warrantor_warrant::BoundStrength`'s sense (`rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:198–212`): no
signature, no process link, no netns, no seccomp, no firewall. **What escapes the chokepoint:** a
warrant minted by any path that does not call `WarrantStore::delegate`; a second store process holding
its own copy of the lineage; a forged or harvested token, which by L6-09's own `what` clause *"routes
around the chain entirely"*; and spend itself, because
`warrantor_warrant::WarrantBounds::budget_cents_observed` is documented `Observed` at
`rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:260–269` — this task refuses the *grant* of a budget the population cannot
support, never the dollar leaving.

**Tier C — observed.** The L6-09 detector is `Observed`. It enumerates complementary pairs and the
population's composed union and reports them; it refuses nothing. The catalog item itself sets this
expectation at line 4230: *"Detection has latency; the window between expansion and alarm is a
published number, not zero."*

**The sentence that ships in the product, next to the guarantee and not in a footnote:**

> Warrantor refuses a delegation whose grant would let a population of sibling agents jointly hold more
> than the ancestor that spawned them — the refusal happens when the warrant is issued, and it names
> the ancestor, both siblings and the numbers. **It does not cover:** agents granted authority by two
> different roots, which never share an ancestor here and compose freely; agents coordinating through
> any channel this system does not mediate; authority obtained by forging or harvesting a credential
> rather than by delegation; and spend, which is measured from the agent's own reporting and not
> refused as the money moves. Two of these have detectors that report after the fact. None of them has
> a bound.

**The orphan count does not rise.** Every crate touched — `warrantor-delegation-chain`,
`warrantor-evidence`, `warrantor-warrant` — is already in the ten reachable from `warrantor-warrant`,
verified above. No new crate is created. `python tools/ci/wiring_census.py` must still print
`10 of 40 crates reachable`.

**No new trust root.** The incompatible-pair register is **unsigned local state on the store**, exactly
the weight of the `revoked: HashSet<String>` that already sits beside it at line 176 and already drives
`is_valid`. It establishes only this: *warrants issued through this store, in this process, were checked
against the pairs this process was told about.* It establishes **nothing** about warrants issued
elsewhere, nothing about a second machine, nothing an auditor can verify without trusting the operator
who configured it, and no fact that crosses an organization — that last is Task 9.5's problem, not a
thing this task quietly solves. Nothing is fetched over a network and no key is introduced.

recorded findings at ceiling 18)` where `N` is the raised floor and the ignored count is still **18**.
A thirteenth `#[ignore]` fails it. A floor raised past what the tests earn fails it. A floor left
unraised while tests are added is caught by review against the captured line.

```rust
  /// The ancestor's ceiling, folded from its own root-first lineage with the one delegation algebra
  /// ([`intersect_chain`]). Deliberately NOT `effective_scope`: that returns a stored field, and a
  /// ceiling read from stored state cannot detect a store whose lineage and scopes disagree.
  pub fn effective_ceiling_of(&self, id: &str) -> Result<WarrantScope, ChainEscalation> {
      let scopes: Vec<WarrantScope> = self.chain_of(id).into_iter().map(|w| w.scope).collect();
      intersect_chain(&scopes)
  }
```

```rust
  #[test]
  fn two_lawful_siblings_compose_a_budget_the_ancestor_never_held() {

      let mut store = WarrantStore::new();

      let first = store.delegate("org", "sib-a",

      assert!(first.is_ok(), "the FIRST grant is lawful and must be allowed; a refusal here would \
          mean the control refuses everything and proves nothing");

      let composed = store.composed_authority("org");
      assert_eq!(composed.committed_budget_micros, 400_000_000);

      let second = store.delegate("org", "sib-b",
          &scope(&["github:write"], &["repo:acme/web"], 900_000, 400_000_000));
      assert!(second.is_err(), "the SECOND grant composes 800 000 000 micros under a 500 000 000 \
          ceiling and must be refused at the moment of the grant, not observed after the fact");
  }
```

```rust
  // in `delegate`, after: let scope = intersection(&parent.scope, requested)?;
  let ceiling = self
      .effective_ceiling_of(parent_id)
      .map_err(|widened| DelegateError::Escalated(widened.escalation))?;
  let composed = self.composed_authority(parent_id);
  let would_commit = composed.committed_budget_micros.saturating_add(scope.budget_micros);
  if would_commit > ceiling.budget_micros {
      return Err(DelegateError::Composed(PopulationEscalation::Budget {
          ancestor: parent_id.to_string(),
          committed_micros: composed.committed_budget_micros,
          requested_micros: scope.budget_micros,
          ceiling_micros: ceiling.budget_micros,
          committed_by: composed.members.clone(),
      }));
  }
```

```rust
  impl std::fmt::Display for PopulationEscalation {
      fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
          match self {
              Self::Budget { ancestor, committed_micros, requested_micros, ceiling_micros,
                             committed_by } => write!(f,
                  "sibling composition under ancestor {ancestor}: {} already commit \
                   {committed_micros} micros and this grant asks {requested_micros} more, which is \
                   {} over the ancestor's ceiling of {ceiling_micros} (authority expansion across \
                   siblings; I-02, L6-12)",
                  committed_by.join(", "),
                  committed_micros.saturating_add(*requested_micros) - ceiling_micros),
              Self::ComplementaryPair { ancestor, holder, holds, requester, requests } => write!(f,
                  "sibling composition under ancestor {ancestor}: {holder} already holds {holds} \
                   and {requester} asks for {requests}, a pair declared incompatible; neither \
                   sibling holds the composition and the ancestor never granted it (L6-12)"),
          }
      }
  }
```

```rust
  #[test]
  fn the_refusal_names_both_siblings_the_ancestor_and_the_arithmetic() {
      let mut store = WarrantStore::new();
      store.issue_root("org", scope(&["github:write"], &["repo:acme/*"], 1_000_000, 500_000_000));
      store.delegate("org", "sib-a",
          &scope(&["github:write"], &["repo:acme/api"], 900_000, 400_000_000)).unwrap();

      // CONTROL: a second sibling whose grant fits under the remaining 100 000 000.
      let mut control_store = store.clone();
      let control = control_store.delegate("org", "sib-b",
          &scope(&["github:write"], &["repo:acme/web"], 900_000, 100_000_000));

      // ATTACK: the same grant, 400 000 000.
      let attacked = store.delegate("org", "sib-b",
          &scope(&["github:write"], &["repo:acme/web"], 900_000, 400_000_000));

      harness_refused(&control, &attacked);   // control Ok, attack Err
      let Err(DelegateError::Composed(escalation)) = attacked else {
          panic!("a sibling composition must fail as Composed, not as a vertical Escalated");
      };
      let text = escalation.to_string();
      for fragment in ["org", "sib-a", "sib-b", "400000000", "500000000", "I-02", "L6-12"] {
          assert!(text.contains(fragment),
              "the refusal must name {fragment} so an operator reading one line knows which two \
               agents and which ancestor: {text}");
      }
  }
```

  Note the attack's own id appears in the message only because `delegate` knows `child_id`; the
  `ComplementaryPair` variant carries `requester` for the same reason. **Test intent:** a refusal
  paired with an allowed control, and a refusal text an operator can act on without a debugger.

- [ ] **Step 7 — The complementary-capability half, declared rather than invented.** L6-12's ceiling is
  not "the ancestor's set" — the ancestor legitimately holds both `secrets:read` and `net:egress`. The
  item's own words are *"unless a warrant explicitly grants the union."* So the composition must be
  **declared** somewhere, and it may not be declared in `WarrantScope`: `Warrant::compute_digest` at
  line 81 covers `(id, scope, parent)`, so a new scope field would change every warrant digest and every
  `links_digest`, breaking Task 1.5's "the proof format is unchanged" gate. It goes on the store,
  unsigned, beside `revoked`.

```rust

  /// same weight of thing as `revoked`: it binds warrants issued through THIS store in THIS process
  /// and establishes nothing about a warrant issued anywhere else. No new trust root -- see
  /// docs/task-evidence/task-9.4.md.
  pub fn declare_incompatible(&mut self, left: &str, right: &str) { /* normalized, sorted pair */ }
```

```rust
  #[test]
  fn a_declared_incompatible_pair_is_refused_at_the_second_grant_with_an_allowed_control() {
      let seed = || {
          let mut store = WarrantStore::new();
          store.issue_root("org",
              scope(&["secrets:read", "net:egress"], &["*"], 1_000_000, 500_000_000));
          store.delegate("org", "reader",
              &scope(&["secrets:read"], &["vault/*"], 900_000, 1_000)).unwrap();
          store
      };

      // CONTROL: nothing declared, so the egress sibling is granted. It is REPORTED (Step 8),
      // not refused -- a control that were refused would prove the check refuses everything.
      let mut permitted = seed();
      let control = permitted.delegate("org", "sender",
          &scope(&["net:egress"], &["https://*"], 900_000, 1_000));
      assert!(control.is_ok(), "an undeclared pair must still be granted; detection is Tier C");

      // ATTACK: the same two siblings with the pair declared.
      let mut guarded = seed();
      guarded.declare_incompatible("secrets:read", "net:egress");
      let attacked = guarded.delegate("org", "sender",
          &scope(&["net:egress"], &["https://*"], 900_000, 1_000));
      let Err(DelegateError::Composed(PopulationEscalation::ComplementaryPair {
          ancestor, holder, holds, requester, requests })) = attacked else {
          panic!("a declared incompatible pair must refuse as ComplementaryPair: {attacked:?}");
      };
      assert_eq!((ancestor.as_str(), holder.as_str(), requester.as_str()),
                 ("org", "reader", "sender"));
      assert_eq!((holds.as_str(), requests.as_str()), ("secrets:read", "net:egress"));

      // And the ancestor holding BOTH is not a grant of the composition.
      assert!(guarded.effective_scope("org").unwrap().capabilities
                  .contains(&"net:egress".to_string()),
          "the ancestor holds both capabilities individually; that is precisely not the same as \
           having granted their composition to a population");
  }
```

  **Test intent:** the refusal fires only on a declaration, the control proves it is not refusing
  everything, and the last assertion pins the semantic distinction the item turns on.

- [ ] **Step 8 — The L6-09 detector, `Observed` and honest about it.** `composed_authority` plus a
  report over a population: the union, the committed budget, the latest expiry, and every complementary
  pair present whether declared or not. It refuses nothing, and its doc comment says so in the tier
  vocabulary so a caller cannot mistake it for a gate.

```rust
  /// Report a population's composed authority and its complementary pairs.
  ///
  /// `BoundStrength::Observed`: this measures and reports, and refuses nothing. Expansion that
  /// routes around delegation entirely -- a forged token, a harvested credential, an account the
  /// model created -- never appears in `parent` links and is therefore invisible here. That is
  /// L6-09's stated residual, not a defect in this function.
  pub fn authority_expansion_report(&self, ancestor: &str) -> PopulationReport;
```

```rust
  #[test]
  fn the_detector_reports_the_undeclared_pair_it_did_not_refuse() {
      let mut store = WarrantStore::new();
      store.issue_root("org", scope(&["secrets:read", "net:egress"], &["*"], 1_000_000, 10_000));
      store.delegate("org", "reader", &scope(&["secrets:read"], &["vault/*"], 900_000, 1)).unwrap();
      store.delegate("org", "sender", &scope(&["net:egress"], &["https://*"], 900_000, 1)).unwrap();

      let report = store.authority_expansion_report("org");
      assert_eq!(report.members, vec!["reader".to_string(), "sender".to_string()]);
      assert!(report.complementary_pairs.iter().any(|p|
              p.left == "secrets:read" && p.right == "net:egress" && !p.declared_incompatible),
          "the population the store DID allow must still be reported, with declared=false, or the \
           only pairs an operator ever sees are the ones already refused");
      assert_eq!(report.union_capabilities,
                 vec!["net:egress".to_string(), "secrets:read".to_string()],
          "the union is what neither sibling holds alone");
      assert!(report.union_capabilities.iter().all(|c|
              store.effective_ceiling_of("org").unwrap().capabilities.contains(c)),
          "and it is within the ancestor's set -- which is why the capability union alone is NOT \
           the finding; the finding is that no sibling holds the composition");
  }
```

  **Test intent:** detection covers exactly the case refusal does not, and the test states in its own
  message why the union-vs-ancestor comparison is not the interesting one.

```rust
      let population = bind_population(&store, "org").expect("the ancestor's population binds");
      assert_eq!(population.ancestor, "org");
      assert!(population.union_capabilities.iter().all(|c|
              authority.chain[0].capabilities.contains(c)),
```

### Task 9.5: Cross-organization authority and agent naming (L6-08, L6-10)

**Anchor.** L6-08 `status=none` `novel` W3; L6-10 `status=none` `align` W4. **The moment authority
crosses an organization, "no new trust root" stops being a preference and becomes the whole design
problem.** Two organizations that must agree on what an agent is authorized to do, without either
becoming the other's certificate authority, is the hardest constraint in the authority plane.

**Step 0.** Read `memory/no-new-trust-root.md`'s rule as it appears in this repository's practice:
build the weaker thing and name what it does not establish. Read Task 1.6 (trust directory bundle
export/import and second-machine verification) in full — that task already solved a smaller version
of this problem and its shape is the precedent to extend, not to reinvent. Read
`rust/trust-core/` and `rust/agent-manifest/` and record what identity crosses a boundary today.
For L6-10, survey existing naming schemes rather than inventing one — it is an `align` item, so the
deliverable is a profile over something that exists.

**Non-goals.** Not a federation service. Not a public key infrastructure. Not the incident-exchange
profile — 14.8. Not jurisdiction modules — 14.5.

**Files.** `rust/trust-core/`, `rust/agent-manifest/`, `docs/task-evidence/task-9.5.md`.

**Consumes / Produces.** Consumes Task 1.6's trust bundle and Task 3.1's principals. Produces a
cross-organization authority profile in which each side verifies out of band, plus a naming and
resolution scheme that does not require a registry.

**Bound strength.** **Tier C, observed,** and this must be stated first rather than last. Without a
shared root, one organization cannot *enforce* anything about another's agent; it can only refuse to
accept what it cannot verify. The honest claim is "we refuse what we cannot verify out of band", not
"authority is portable across organizations".

**Exit gate.** Two organizations exchange an authority claim, each verifies it against a bundle
pinned out of band, and a claim signed by an unpinned key is **refused**; and the design document
states in one paragraph what this does not establish, in the same words as Task 1.6's.

### Task 9.6: Attested sender identity and the channel policy language (L5-06, L5-05)

**Anchor.** L5-06 is `status=none`, `core`, W2: cryptographic sender attestation bound to the agent
principal, *"verified by the broker before delivery, so impersonation is unrepresentable rather than
detectable."* L5-05 is `status=none`, `core`, W2: who may message whom, about which classes, at what
rate, with what disclosure — expressed in the same policy language as egress and compiled by the
same compiler, *"so one document governs both."* The blueprint anchors both to the METR/Redwood
observation that the agents' message board was unauthenticated and names could be posted by anyone.

This task is first in Phase 9's channel group because every collusion control above it — 9.7's
cross-tenant firewall, 9.4's sibling-collusion intersection, 6.2's swarm detection — assumes it can
tell one agent's message from another's.

**The finding that sets this task's real size.** Searched across `origin/main` for
`peer_proposal`, `PeerProposal`, `fn send_message`, `struct Message` and `agent_to_agent`:
**zero hits in any Rust crate.** There is no channel plane. There is no broker to verify before
delivery, no message type to attest, and no delivery path to refuse on. L5-06's phrase *"verified
by the broker before delivery"* presumes infrastructure that does not exist.

So this is not "add a signature to messages." It is **the channel plane's first task**, and it must
be scoped as such or it will silently become three tasks. What exists to build on:
`rust/trust-core/src/cli.rs` has Ed25519 `key-gen`, `sign` and `verify` fully wired (lines 4–91,
`ed25519_dalek`), and `rust/notary/src/lib.rs:325` has a `SignatureEnvelope` — `algorithm`,
`key_id`, `public_key`, `value` — already used for receipts. **Reuse `SignatureEnvelope`.** A second
signature envelope shape in one system is a verification bug waiting to be written.

**Step 0.** Run and capture verbatim:

```
git grep -n "peer_proposal\|PeerProposal\|fn send_message\|struct Message" origin/main -- 'rust/**/*.rs'
git show origin/main:rust/notary/src/lib.rs | sed -n '320,352p'
git show origin/main:rust/trust-core/src/cli.rs | sed -n '1,40p'
```

Read in full: `rust/trust-core/src/lib.rs` and `cli.rs` for the key model; `rust/notary/src/lib.rs`
lines 320–400 for `SignatureEnvelope` and `canonical_receipt_body` — the canonicalization rule is
reusable and re-deriving it is how two signers stop agreeing; the egress policy language this task
must extend rather than parallel (Task 1.2's capability-derived destinations, Task 2.5's destination
catalog); and Task 3.1's agent-principal grains, because the attestation binds to a principal that
task defines.

**Non-goals.**
- Not coordination primitives or the cross-tenant firewall — Task 9.7.
- Not peer-proposal admission — that is a consumer of this, and it is Task 2.6's provenance work
  plus Phase 9's later tasks.
- Not a transport. Task 9.9 profiles A2A and MCP; this task defines what any transport must carry.
- Not a message broker as a service. **No new trust root:** build the local verifier and state
  precisely what it does not establish — specifically, that it cannot prove a message was *not*
  delivered elsewhere.

**Files.** A new `rust/channel/` crate, `rust/notary/src/lib.rs` (read-only — reuse
`SignatureEnvelope`, do not modify it), `rust/warrant/Cargo.toml` (wiring edge, contended),
`docs/W1-delivery-gaps.md`, `docs/task-evidence/task-9.6.md`.

**Consumes / Produces.** Consumes `SignatureEnvelope` (`rust/notary/src/lib.rs:325`),
`canonical_receipt_body`'s canonicalization discipline, `SigningKey` from `ed25519_dalek` as used in
`rust/trust-core/src/cli.rs:90`, and the agent principal from Task 3.1. Produces an
`AttestedMessage` type and a `verify_before_delivery` function that is the only path to delivery,
plus a channel clause in the policy grammar compiled by the same compiler as egress.

**Bound strength.** **Tier B, chokepoint.** Attestation binds only messages that traverse this
broker. Two agents sharing a filesystem, a database table, a shared model context or any
side channel exchange unattested messages, and this control cannot see them. State that in those
words — it is the same limit Task 3.6's improvised-channel detection exists to partially cover, and
the two tasks must not each claim the other closes it.

**Exit gate.** A message whose sender field does not match its signature is refused **at the
delivery function**, not flagged after; and one policy document, compiled once, produces both an
egress decision and a channel decision — demonstrated by a test that compiles a single document and
asserts on both outputs.

### Task 9.7: Cross-tenant channel firewall and coordination primitives (L5-09, L5-07)

### Task 10.1: The causal verdict — STRICT_CAUSAL, made real (L7-01)

**Anchor.** L7-01 is `status=none`, `novel`, W2. Quoted verbatim from the master blueprint,
`docs/html/warrantor-native-ai-platform-os-master-2026-09-01.html:4276`:

Its `what` clause, line 4280, is the whole specification:

> A verdict that validates the pathway to an outcome, not merely the outcome. "Right result, wrong
> route" is a violation. The receipt records which authority, which effects, in which order,
> produced the result, and the verdict is computed over that chain rather than over a final
> assertion.

Its `why` clause, line 4281, is why it leads Phase 10: *"This is the highest-leverage single item in
the catalog. Hundreds of agents spent days building tooling to defeat a causal check they believed
existed; it did not."* Its proof gate is F-02, line 4283: *"Produce a correct outcome by an
unauthorized route and assert the verdict is a violation, per effect class."* And its own recorded
residual, line 4284, is the sentence this task must not let the product forget: *"Pathway checking
depends on evidence completeness; gaps in F-04 become gaps here."*

`status=none` is correct as a statement about the verdict. It is **not** correct as a statement about
the data. Four things the seed treats as absent are already on `origin/main`, and the expansion below
is a different task because of it.

**Premise contradicted — five corrections, and one confirmation.**

`staged_tools` is collected into a `BTreeSet` at `:641–645`, so gate 5 sees *which tools* and never
*which hop, in what order, depending on what*. A three-hop chain whose middle hop is unauthorized and
whose outcome is permitted denies here **only if** that middle tool is outside `bounds.tools`. If it
is inside — the common case, since a warrant grants a tool set and the route through it is
unconstrained — the union is satisfied, gate 5 allows, and the report's one question has been answered
correctly about a route nobody checked. That is the defect, stated precisely, and it is why Step 4's
adversarial chain has to keep the *outcome* permitted while breaking a *hop*.

**The refusal shape to imitate.** `evidence::verify_chain` already refuses a broken link by name and
by value, `rust/evidence/src/lib.rs:505–518`:

```rust
    match &post_commit.predicate.binding.parent_receipt {
```

Note what it does: it distinguishes *wrong parent* from *no parent*, and the second string is asserted

`rust/warrant/tests/invariants/i07_evidence_precedes_commitment.rs:33`. `CausalRefusal` must be that
specific — `UnauthorizedHop` and `OrderBroken` are separate variants for the same reason, and each
must name its index, because "the chain is bad" is not an auditable refusal.

**The order the signature must carry.** `release_order` at `rust/warrant/src/staging.rs:463–473` is
the order Step 5 signs, and its doc comment states the property that makes the causal verdict
meaningful at all:

```rust

    /// Every prefix of this order is a coherent state, which is what makes a partial release

```

Sign *this* order, not the staging order. They differ whenever an agent stages out of dependency
sequence, and the release order is the one the settle engine at `rust/warrant/src/settle.rs:136`
actually executes. A causal verdict computed over the staging order would be a verdict about an order
that never runs.

`premise_contradicted = true`. The seed's finding about the verdict is right; its finding about the

**A defect to fix in Step 3, found while reading.** `ReceiptBody` derives plain `Deserialize` with no
`#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. Serde silently drops unknown fields. So a v2 body handed to a v1
`verify_receipt` deserializes, loses the new fields, re-canonicalizes without them, and fails as
`NotaryError::InvalidSignature` — a version mismatch reported to a third-party auditor as a forgery.
The same hole exists on `WarPredicate`. Whatever version field this task adds must be read *before*
the signature check and must produce its own error variant.

```rust
pub struct DualSignedPayload {
    /// Canonical-JSON payload (the thing being signed).
    pub payload: serde_json::Value,
    /// Classical signature (Ed25519) — present now.
    pub classical: SignatureEntry,
    /// Post-quantum signature (ML-DSA or SLH-DSA) — present when PQ keys are available.
    /// None = "PQ-ready but not yet PQ-signed" (the migration window).
    pub post_quantum: Option<SignatureEntry>,
}
```

10.9 adds signature *entries beside* an opaque payload. 10.1 adds fields *inside* the payload. They
compose, in either order, and neither reads the other's bytes. **The real collision risk is
different and worth writing down:** `post-quantum` carries a third independent canonicalizer
(`canonical_json`, `:328`) alongside `notary::canonical_receipt_body` (`:453`) and
`evidence::canonical_predicate` (`:255`). Three implementations of one security-critical function,
which spec 11 §1 forbids for security invariants. This task must not add a fourth. Say so in the
evidence file and leave the consolidation to whichever task owns it.

**Bound strength.** **Tier C — Observed.** State it bluntly; this item's prominence in the blueprint
is exactly what invites overclaiming, and `BoundStrength` at `rust/warrant/src/lib.rs:197–211`
reserves `Enforced` for cryptography and the operating system and `Mediated` for the proxy
chokepoint. The causal verdict is neither. It refuses at settle time, over a record; nothing refuses
an effect at the moment the agent attempts it, because the effects are queued rather than executed.
That containment is real and it is not enforcement.

> reachable from the command line — so a route that never passed through the staging queue is

### Task 10.2: Receipt query language and live stream (L7-13)

**Anchor.** L7-13 is `status=none`, `core`, W2: a stable query surface over the graph and a
resumable live stream of settled receipts, *"so audit, detection, corpus extraction and regulator
access all read the same structure through one interface rather than four pipelines."* The
blueprint's compounding argument is five consumers over one structure.

Those five consumers are already scheduled and they are the reason this task is substrate: Task
11.4's audit workbench, Task 11.9's regulator portal, Task 12.1's corpus extraction, Task 6.2's
swarm detection on the receipt graph, and Task 11.13's natural-language console. **If this task
does not land first, each of those five builds its own reader**, and the blueprint's margin
argument inverts into five pipelines to keep in agreement.

**What exists.** `rust/notary/src/lib.rs:336` defines `ReceiptBody` and `WarReceipt`. The only
thing resembling a query surface on `origin/main` is `rust/archive/src/bin/warrantor-archive.rs`.
There is no index, no filter grammar, and no stream. `rust/archive/` also carries the append-only
and device-pairing tests that pin what the archive may and may not do — read them before designing,
because *"the archive never serves a verdict"* is an existing test name and it is a constraint on
this task: the query surface returns receipts, and a caller computes verdicts from them.

**The ordering dependency, stated so it is not discovered late.** Task 10.1 changes the signed
receipt body to carry a chain. **A query language frozen against the v1 shape will need breaking
changes the week 10.1 lands.** Either 10.1 lands first, or this task's grammar is explicitly
versioned from its first commit and its tests pin both shapes. Choose in Step 0 and record the
choice; do not leave it implicit.

**Bound strength.** **Tier C, observed.** A query surface is a read path; it enforces nothing. Its
one real guarantee is that two consumers asking the same question get the same answer, and that is
worth asserting directly rather than assuming — a differential test across two consumers is the
strongest thing this task can claim.

**Exit gate.** Two different consumers issue the same query and receive byte-identical results; a
stream interrupted mid-read resumes from its cursor with no gap and no duplicate, proven by a test
that kills the reader mid-stream rather than by a comment saying it is resumable.

### Task 10.5: Exception, waiver and compensating-control lifecycle; control-effectiveness sampling (L7-16, L7-17)

**Anchor.** L7-16 `core` W2; L7-17 `novel` W3; both `status=none`. **Every real deployment grants
exceptions.** An exception with no expiry and no compensating control is a silent policy edit — and it
is the mechanism by which a governed system becomes an ungoverned one without anybody deciding to.

**Step 0.** Read the policy path and record whether any exception mechanism exists today; if operators
currently achieve exceptions by editing policy, that is the finding and it belongs in the anchor. Read
the already-seeded Task 8.2 (risk dial) — a dial loosening and an exception are close cousins, so
record whether they are one mechanism. Read `docs/W1-delivery-gaps.md` for the disclosure habit these
records should follow.

Task 13.8.

**Consumes / Produces.** Consumes the policy engine. Produces exceptions that **must** carry an expiry
and a compensating control, expire automatically, and are sampled for effectiveness on a schedule.

**Bound strength.** **Tier B, chokepoint.** An exception without an expiry cannot be created — that is
a real refusal point. Effectiveness sampling is **Tier C, observed**.

**Exit gate.** An exception without an expiry or a compensating control is **refused at creation**,
with a complete one accepted; an expired exception stops taking effect without anybody acting; and
sampling produces a record for each active exception.

*(c) What append-only guarantees exist today, and at which tier.* Four mechanisms, and the crate's own

> `UPDATE`/`DELETE` grant — because a grant can be misconfigured by an operator and a trigger cannot.
> [...] It is worth being exact about the limit. Append-only is a property of the *application role*,
> not of the storage: whoever owns the database can delete rows out of band, and no trigger stops them.
> What actually carries the custody guarantee is that the artifacts are independently verifiable off
> this archive, against an anchor the reader pinned.

**Does custody bind to the v1 `ReceiptBody` or to Task 10.1's shape? Neither.** It binds to the filed
bytes and their SHA-256, and to two field *names* on `Binding` (`receipt_id`, `parent_receipt`, lines
127 and 131) that 10.1 does not rename. Task 10.1 has **not landed**. What breaks if 10.1 lands first:
**nothing in the custody digest, and exactly one thing in the fixtures.** A custody fixture that
*rebuilds* a `WarPredicate` and hashes the result will change digest the moment `predicate_version`
becomes the predicate's first field. Every fixture in this task therefore freezes bytes as `const`
string literals and never recomputes, which is the same discipline Task 10.1's own Step 2 requires of
its canonical vectors: *"A fixture that recomputes the canonical form proves nothing about a format
change, because it recomputes it under the new rule."* If 10.6 lands first, 10.1 needs no change here
either — `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` on `ReceiptBody` cannot break a verifier that never
deserializes one.

Produces, all new:

```rust
// rust/evidence/src/custody.rs
pub const CUSTODY_FORMAT: &str = "warrantor.custody-act/1";
pub const MANIFEST_FORMAT: &str = "warrantor.escrow-manifest/1";

/// One evidence handoff. `prev` chains it; `digest` is over every field above `digest`.
pub struct CustodyAct { pub format: String, pub artifact_digest: String,
                        pub from_party: String, pub to_party: String,
                        pub purpose: String, pub at: u64,
                        pub prev: String, pub digest: String }
pub struct CustodyHead { pub acts: usize, pub head: Option<String>, pub chain_intact: bool }
pub fn append_act(prior: Option<&CustodyAct>, artifact_digest: &str, from_party: &str,
                  to_party: &str, purpose: &str, at: u64) -> CustodyAct;
pub fn verify_custody_chain(acts: &[CustodyAct]) -> Result<CustodyHead, EvidenceError>;

/// The enumeration. `sequence` is monotone per escrow; `prev_manifest` chains generations.
pub struct EscrowManifest { pub format: String, pub sequence: u64,
                            pub members: Vec<String>, pub custody_head: Option<String>,
                            pub prev_manifest: String, pub sealed_at: u64 }
pub struct SealedManifest { pub manifest: EscrowManifest, pub signature: SignatureEnvelope }
pub fn seal(manifest: EscrowManifest, key: &SigningKey, key_id: &str) -> SealedManifest;

/// What an investigator receives: the seal, the custody chain, and the bytes.
pub struct Release { pub sealed: SealedManifest, pub custody: Vec<CustodyAct>,
                     pub artifacts: BTreeMap<String, Vec<u8>> }

pub enum ReleaseRefusal {
    MemberWithheld { digest: String, sequence: u64 },
    DigestMismatch { claimed: String, actual: String },
    ManifestSignature(String),
    ManifestNotSignedByAnchor { pinned: String, presented: String },
    CustodyChainBroken { index: usize, expected: String, found: String },
    CustodyHeadMismatch { manifest_says: Option<String>, chain_says: Option<String> },
    TruncatedBelowPin { pinned: u64, presented: u64 },
}

/// What the release DOES and DOES NOT establish. `not_covered` is never empty.
pub struct ReleaseCoverage { pub members: usize, pub verified: usize,
                             pub manifest_sequence: u64, pub tail_pinned: bool,
                             pub not_covered: Vec<&'static str> }
impl ReleaseCoverage { pub fn sentence(&self) -> String; }

pub fn verify_release(release: &Release, anchor: &VerifyingKey,
                      pinned_sequence: Option<u64>) -> Result<ReleaseCoverage, ReleaseRefusal>;

// rust/evidence/src/lib.rs — two variants added to the existing enum at :212
    #[error("custody chain broken at act {0}")] CustodyChain(usize),
    #[error("escrow manifest malformed: {0}")] Manifest(String),

// rust/archive/src/store.rs — one read method on the trait, and one write that marks
    fn is_sealed(&self, digest: &str) -> Result<bool, StoreError>;
    fn seal(&mut self, digest: &str, manifest_sequence: u64, at: u64) -> Result<(), StoreError>;

// rust/warrant/src/report.rs — an OPTIONAL section, so v1 bundle digests are unchanged
pub struct EscrowSection { pub manifest_sequence: u64, pub members: usize,
                           pub custody_head: Option<String>, pub sealed_by_key_id: String }
```

**No new trust root.** There is no escrow service, no notary-of-notaries, no neutral third party, and no
network call anywhere in `verify_release`. The escrow is a local file the operator produces and the
sequence pin is a **number the investigator wrote down**, obtainable two ways that already exist: from a
prior release the investigator holds (sequence is monotone, so a second release presenting a lower one
is refused), or from a `CustodySection.head` already inside a separately-held signed report. What this
establishes: any release at or below a sequence the investigator has independently seen is complete
relative to its own manifest, and any custody gap in it is detectable offline. What it does **not**
establish: anything at all about the first release an investigator ever receives, and nothing about
generations the operator sealed and never disclosed.

---

**Bound strength.** Split three ways, because one label over these three properties would be a lie.

**Tier A — cryptographic, refused at the moment of attempt.** Three properties. (1) *Tamper-evidence of
an escrowed artifact*: the manifest member list is SHA-256 digests inside an Ed25519-signed manifest, so
an altered artifact fails `DigestMismatch` at the line that recomputes it, and an altered manifest fails
`ManifestSignature`. (2) *Withholding a member of a disclosed manifest*: a release carrying fewer
artifacts than its manifest enumerates is refused with `MemberWithheld` naming the missing digest — the
verifier returns `Err`, it does not warn. (3) *A missing custody transition*: `verify_custody_chain`
refuses `CustodyChainBroken` when act *n*'s `prev` is not act *n−1*'s `digest`, which is L7-08's
verification clause, *"a custody transition missing from the chain fails verification at the receiving
party,"* made executable. All three are conditional on the investigator holding the issuer key out of
band — `verify_export` is anchor-free by construction and
`rust/archive/tests/verification_does_not_depend_on_the_archive.rs:292` already asserts in both
directions that a bundle signed end to end by any keypair passes it. `verify_release` therefore takes
`anchor: &VerifyingKey` as a required argument, not an option.

**Tier C — observed, and in one case not even that.** *Completeness of the manifest itself.* Nothing
here proves the operator escrowed everything. An operator who never sealed a trace produces a release
that verifies perfectly and omits it, and no examination of the release reveals the omission. The one
partial mitigation is `TruncatedBelowPin`, and it fires only when the investigator supplies a
`pinned_sequence` from a source outside this release — so it is Tier A **at and below the pin** and gives
nothing above it or before it. `ReleaseCoverage.not_covered` is never empty and
`ReleaseCoverage::sentence()` renders it, in the register `Coverage::sentence()` uses at
`rust/warrant/src/harness.rs:79`.

**Not Tier A: the store.** `rust/archive`'s append-only is Tier A at the trigger and Tier A for the
runtime role's grants, and the crate's own doc is right that *"whoever owns the database can delete rows
out of band, and no trigger stops them"* (`rust/archive/src/lib.rs:50–52`). The seal is a marker a
retention pass consults, not a lock. **`is_sealed` refuses nothing.** Task 10.4 owns any refusal built
on it. There is no netns, seccomp or firewall anywhere in this repository and nothing in this task adds
one; no bound here is claimed at the operating system.

**The sentence that appears in the product**, added to `limitations()` at
`rust/warrant/src/report.rs:545` alongside the existing set:

> Escrowed evidence is tamper-evident and its disclosed set is complete: an altered artifact, an altered
> manifest, a missing custody transition or a withheld member of a sealed manifest each fail
> verification at the receiving party, offline, against a key that party pinned. **This does not prove
> everything was escrowed.** The manifest says what was sealed, and nothing in a release says what was
> not. An operator who never sealed a trace produces a release that verifies and omits it, and a release
> truncated at its most recent generation is indistinguishable from a release that is current unless you
> already know a later sequence number. Read a release as complete relative to its own manifest, never
> as complete relative to what happened.

**No claim without a mechanism.** Every clause above has one: `ReleaseRefusal::MemberWithheld`
(refusal), `ReleaseRefusal::CustodyChainBroken` (refusal), `ReleaseRefusal::TruncatedBelowPin`
(refusal), `ReleaseCoverage::not_covered` (generated text), and `limitations()` (shipped file).

**The orphan count may not rise, and does not.** No crate is created. `rust/evidence` is already
reachable; `rust/archive` is already an orphan and **stays** one — this task neither un-orphans it nor
adds a new one. `python tools/ci/wiring_census.py` must still print `10 of 40 crates reachable from
warrantor-warrant over 18 path edges`. Adding `pub mod custody;` to a crate already in the reachable set
adds no edge.

**No recorded invariant violation is converted by this task.** The eighteen `#[ignore]`s in
`rust/warrant/tests/invariants/` are I-01 (2), I-03 (4), I-04 (2), I-05 (2), I-06 (1), I-08 (2), I-09
(1), I-10 (1), I-11 (2) and I-12 (1); none concerns custody, escrow or investigator access.
`tools/ci/invariant-ratchet.json` is therefore **not edited**: `passing_floor` stays 66 and
`ignored_ceiling` stays 18, and the evidence file records the captured line `invariant ratchet: ok (66
passing at floor 66, 18 recorded findings at ceiling 18)` both before and after, read from the tool
output rather than computed. A nineteenth ignore anywhere raises the ceiling and fails the build, which
is the correct outcome.

---

**Exit gate.** One command decides it:

```

cargo test -p warrantor-archive --test append_only --test verification_does_not_depend_on_the_archive --test escrow_release_verifies_off_the_archive && \
cd M:/wt-10.6 && python tools/ci/wiring_census.py && python tools/ci/check_invariant_ratchet.py
```

Pass requires all five of: `custody_and_escrow` showing at least seven refusals each with its allowed
control and `0 failed`; `append_only` still `7 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored`;
`verification_does_not_depend_on_the_archive` still `6 passed; 0 failed`;
`escrow_release_verifies_off_the_archive` passing with no `warrantor_archive` type in the verify call
graph; and the last two lines reading exactly `wiring census: 10 of 40 crates reachable from
warrantor-warrant over 18 path edges` and `invariant ratchet: ok (66 passing at floor 66, 18 recorded
findings at ceiling 18)`. Any other number on either tool line is a failure regardless of the tests.

      ```rust
      #[test]
      fn a_missing_custody_transition_fails_verification_at_the_receiving_party() {
          // vendor -> customer -> supervisor -> investigator: the handoff L7-08 names.
          let a = append_act(None, FILED_DIGEST, "vendor", "customer", "contractual audit", NOW);
          let b = append_act(Some(&a), FILED_DIGEST, "customer", "supervisor", "examination", NOW + 60);
          let c = append_act(Some(&b), FILED_DIGEST, "supervisor", "investigator", "incident", NOW + 120);

          // -- the CONTROL: the whole chain verifies and the head is the last act ---------
          let head = verify_custody_chain(&[a.clone(), b.clone(), c.clone()])
              .expect("an intact three-hop chain must verify");
          assert_eq!(head.acts, 3);
          assert!(head.chain_intact);
          assert_eq!(head.head.as_deref(), Some(c.digest.as_str()));

          // -- the ATTACK: remove the MIDDLE hop, which is the one an operator would remove
          let refusal = verify_custody_chain(&[a.clone(), c.clone()])
              .expect_err("a chain with a transition removed must not verify");
          match refusal {
              EvidenceError::CustodyChain(index) => assert_eq!(
                  index, 1,
                  "the refusal must name WHICH transition is missing, at the receiving party's end"
              ),
              other => panic!("expected CustodyChain, got {other}"),
          }

          // -- and an EDITED act is the same refusal, not a silent pass -------------------
          let mut edited = b.clone();
          edited.to_party = "a party that never held it".to_string();
          verify_custody_chain(&[a, edited, c])
              .expect_err("an edited act must not verify: its digest no longer covers its contents");
      }
      ```

      *Test intent:* two refusals and one control. The middle hop is removed deliberately — removing the
      tail is the case Step 7 proves is *not* detectable, and conflating the two is exactly the overclaim
      Correction 6 is about.

      ```rust
      #[test]
      fn a_manifest_sealed_by_the_operators_own_key_is_refused_against_the_pinned_anchor() {
          let anchor = issuer().verifying_key();
          let manifest = escrow_manifest_naming(&[FILED_DIGEST]);

          // The operator seals a manifest saying whatever it likes, with a VALID key it holds.
          // Nothing is inconsistent: the signature verifies against the key it carries.
          let forged = seal(manifest.clone(), &operator_key(), "operator");
          let release = Release { sealed: forged, custody: vec![], artifacts: one_artifact() };

          let refusal = verify_release(&release, &anchor, None).expect_err(
              "a manifest signed by a key that is not the pinned issuer must not verify -- this is \
               the attack that `verification_does_not_depend_on_the_archive.rs:299` already asserts \
               for bundles, and a release is a bundle-of-bundles with the same hole",
          );
          match refusal {
              ReleaseRefusal::ManifestNotSignedByAnchor { pinned, presented } => {
                  assert_eq!(pinned, hex::encode(anchor.to_bytes()),
                      "the refusal must name the key the reader pinned, so they can tell a \
                       wrong-signer from a tampered file");
                  assert_ne!(pinned, presented);
              }
              other => panic!("expected ManifestNotSignedByAnchor, got {other:?}"),
          }

          // The CONTROL: the same manifest sealed by the real issuer verifies.
          let genuine = seal(manifest, &issuer(), "issuer");
          verify_release(
              &Release { sealed: genuine, custody: vec![], artifacts: one_artifact() },
              &anchor, None,
          ).expect("sealed by the pinned issuer, it verifies");
      }
      ```

      *Test intent:* one refusal naming both keys, one control. `verify_release` takes the anchor as a
      required argument for this reason — an optional anchor is a hole, and the archive crate learned
      that already.

      ```rust
      #[test]
      fn a_truncated_release_verifies_without_a_pin_and_is_refused_with_one() {
          let anchor = issuer().verifying_key();
          // Generation 9 is current. Generation 4 is a real, genuine, complete, sealed release --
          // and it is also what an operator serves to hide five generations of evidence.
          let stale = release_at_sequence(4);

          // -- Half one: with NO pin it VERIFIES, and that is the honest outcome. There is
          //    nothing wrong with the file. An offline verifier holding one release cannot
          //    distinguish "current" from "truncated". Asserting Ok here is what stops a future
          //    refactor from claiming a detection that does not exist.
          let coverage = verify_release(&stale, &anchor, None)
              .expect("a genuine older generation is a genuine file and must verify");
          assert!(!coverage.tail_pinned);
          assert!(
              coverage.not_covered.iter().any(|s| s.contains("truncat")),
              "with no pin, the coverage report MUST say that truncation is undetectable. \
               not_covered was: {:?}", coverage.not_covered
          );
          assert!(
              coverage.sentence().contains("does not prove everything was escrowed"),
              "the rendered sentence is the product's claim; it must not be silent about this"
          );

          // -- Half two: with a pin the investigator obtained elsewhere, it IS refused. This is
          //    the ONLY mechanism by which withholding a whole generation is detectable, and it
          //    needs a number from outside the release -- no new trust root, a number written down.
          let refusal = verify_release(&stale, &anchor, Some(9)).expect_err(
              "presented below a sequence the investigator has already seen, a release is refused",
          );
          assert!(matches!(
              refusal,
              ReleaseRefusal::TruncatedBelowPin { pinned: 9, presented: 4 }
          ), "got {refusal:?}");

          // -- The CONTROL for half two: at or above the pin, it verifies. ----------------
          verify_release(&release_at_sequence(9), &anchor, Some(9))
              .expect("at the pin, a release verifies");
      }
      ```

      ```rust
      fn a_coverage_report_can_never_render_an_empty_not_covered_list() {
      ```

### Task 10.7: Reasoning-trace monitoring and analysis-of-analysis (L7-11, L7-21)

**Anchor.** L7-11 `compose` W3; L7-21 `novel` W2; both `status=none`. **A monitor that reads
reasoning creates a training incentive to hide reasoning.** That is not a side effect to manage — it
is the central design fact, and it is why L7-21 exists: sampled human verification and second-model
disagreement are the only checks on the checker.

**Step 0.** Read the ML lane's measured results and carry them in rather than re-deriving them:
adversarial phrasing quadruples false-positive rate; evasion is asymmetric at 1.42x, p≈1e-5;
severity instability was the dominant failure mode across all five trained recipes; category
specialization measurably hurt. Read `python/warrantor_ml/src/warrantor_ml/evaluate.py` and
`baselines.py` for the existing evaluation shape. Read Task 12.4 (adversarial-phrasing robustness) —
**that task owns the robustness gate**; this one consumes it.

**Non-goals.** Not building a reasoning model. Not the guard model itself — Phase 12. Not treating a
trace as evidence of intent. Not a claim that monitored reasoning is faithful reasoning.

**Files.** A monitoring integration module, `python/warrantor_ml/`, `docs/task-evidence/task-10.7.md`.

**Consumes / Produces.** Consumes traces where a harness exposes them, and Task 12.4's robustness
gate. Produces a monitor with a **mandatory** sampled-human-verification rate and a second-model
disagreement measure published alongside every monitor verdict.

**Bound strength.** **Tier C, observed,** and additionally **contested**: a trace monitor's output is
weaker than it looks because the trace is generated by the system being monitored. Every number this
produces carries its configuration — context length, seed, quantization — because each changes it,
and quantization changes verdicts at the deployed Q4_K_M.

**Exit gate.** No monitor verdict is publishable without its sampled-verification rate and its
second-model disagreement rate attached, enforced by a test that rejects a verdict missing either;
and the product text states that a monitored trace is not a faithful trace.
